source: Huang et al. (2023) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Asking a model to review its own answer (an assumption check on itself) without outside feedback did not help and often hurt. Models flip right answers to wrong ones.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 after one self-correct round, 41.8 after two. GSM8K 75.9 -> 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Same-model critique with no oracle label. 2023 models; some sets sampled (200 questions, 100 for HotpotQA).
agent_relevance: Supports G2 and G1: a scheduled 'check your assumptions' pass by the same model is not safe. Critique must be tied to real failing output.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction
finding: Survey of self-correction work. Finds no prior work shows successful self-correction using feedback from a prompted LLM, except on tasks unusually suited to it. Works well when reliable external feedback exists.
numbers: Qualitative survey; abstract states the conclusions (prompted-LLM feedback fails outside special tasks; external feedback works).
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Survey, not new experiments. Many positive results used oracle labels or weak baselines.
agent_relevance: Backs the rule that code or tools supply the signal for revision, and the model only fixes. A devil's advocate played by the same model is weak evidence.

source: Liang et al. (2023/2024) Encouraging Divergent Thinking in LLMs through Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Self-reflection suffers 'Degeneration-of-Thought': once confident, the model does not generate new views. Two debaters in 'tit for tat' with a judge (an angel/devil set-up, close to devil's advocacy) beat self-reflection.
numbers: Counter-Intuitive Arithmetic accuracy: GPT-3.5 26.0, +CoT 28.0, +Self-Consistency 29.5, +Self-Reflect 27.5, +MAD 37.0, GPT-4 51.0. On Common MT, GPT-3.5 with MAD matches or beats GPT-4 (human score 3.78 vs 3.41 on one test set). Forcing 'disagree on every point' (disagreement 0.988) was not best.
limits: Two tasks, ChatGPT-class models, judge is also an LLM. Too much forced disagreement hurt (polarisation).
agent_relevance: A devil's advocate role works best at moderate strength and where the first answer is intuitive but wrong. Link to G1: trigger on disagreement, not by schedule.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? Multi-Agent Debate Strategies for LLMs
finding: Large benchmark of debate protocols. No debate protocol beats the non-debate Medprompt on medical QA. Multi-Persona (angel vs devil) was about 7% worse than Medprompt. How strongly the devil disagrees is a hidden knob that changes results a lot.
numbers: Best MAD configs about 61% on MedQA; Medprompt best overall and cheaper. Multi-Persona consistently about 7% below Medprompt. Tuning agreement via the devil prompt gave +15% for Multi-Persona and +5% for Society of Minds on a 376-question USMLE subset. On the counter-intuitive set (CIAR) more disagreement helped; on MedQA and PubMedQA more agreement helped.
limits: Medical and reasoning QA, GPT-3.5 era. Single-agent and self-consistency results swing with prompt wording.
agent_relevance: Best devil strength depends on the task, so a fixed devil is risky. G4 and G5: do not trust debate agreement or a prompt-set disagreement level.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key?
finding: A single agent with a strong prompt gets almost the same result as the best multi-agent discussion. Discussion helps mainly when there are no demonstrations in the prompt.
numbers: Compared Debate, MAD, ReConcile and the authors' CMD against single-agent prompts on several reasoning sets with ChatGPT-3.5 and other backbones. Headline is qualitative in the abstract; per-task numbers not recorded.
limits: Mostly ChatGPT-3.5 and a few other backbones.
agent_relevance: Role-play adversaries add little over a good prompt with examples. Cheap to test before building.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: Several model copies answer, read each other's answers and revise over rounds. This beat single answer, reflection and majority vote.
numbers: 3 agents, 2 rounds, gpt-3.5-turbo. Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8. Grade school math: 77.0, 75.0, 81.0, 85.0. Chess move quality: 91.4, 102.1, 102.2, 122.9.
limits: Same model in all roles, so errors are correlated. Later work (Smit, Wang) finds smaller gains against strong baselines.
agent_relevance: The strongest pro-debate result. Reflection helped little; the gain came from exchange across copies.

source: Khan et al. (2024) Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers
finding: Two expert models argue for different answers and a weaker judge picks. Adversarial debate beat a single consultant and a naive judge. Training debaters to be more persuasive raised judge accuracy.
numbers: QuALITY reading task: debate gives 76% (non-expert LLM judges) and 88% (human judges); naive baselines 48% and 60%. Humans beat LLM judges across protocols. Experts used best-of-16 with GPT-4-Turbo.
limits: Experts hold the source text, judges do not. Closed-book comprehension, not open-world analysis.
agent_relevance: Forcing a second side to argue the opposite answer helps a judge who cannot check facts. This is the machine form of competing hypotheses, with a neutral or code judge.

source: Chen et al. (2023) ReConcile: Round-Table Conference Improves Reasoning via Consensus among Diverse LLMs
finding: Mixing different model families (ChatGPT, Bard, Claude2) with confidence-weighted voting gave larger gains than copies of one model. Diversity of agents was the main source of gain.
numbers: Abstract: beats prior single-agent and multi-agent baselines by up to 11.4% on reasoning, beats GPT-4 on StrategyQA by 3.4%, and beats GPT-4 and DeepSeekMath on MATH by 8%. Response diversity checked with BERTScore.
limits: Needs several vendors. Gain versus same-model copies comes from the authors' own ablation.
agent_relevance: Supports G4 in positive form: only truly different models give independent views. Same-model persona voters do not.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Unleashing Emergent Cognitive Synergy in LLMs: Solo Performance Prompting
finding: One model plays several fine-grained personas that brainstorm and give feedback, like a one-person panel. It reduced factual errors on trivia writing and kept reasoning on logic puzzles, but only in GPT-4, not GPT-3.5 or Llama2-13b.
numbers: Three tasks: Trivia Creative Writing, Codenames Collaborative, Logic Grid Puzzle. Early-termination counts for the fixed-persona variant: 18/100 and 16/100 trivia runs with a system message vs 0/100 and 1/100 without; Codenames 37/50 vs 4/50.
limits: Capability gate: effect appears only in the strongest model. Score table not extracted.
agent_relevance: A persona brainstorm inside one call works only for strong models. Gate it on model strength and measure it.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Models give in when challenged and when a user states a belief. This undermines any devil's advocate asked to judge or revise.
numbers: Asking 'Are you sure?' drops accuracy by up to 27% (Claude 1.3) on average across datasets; models change their first answer between 32% (GPT-4) and 86% (Claude 1.3) of the time. A user suggesting a wrong answer cuts accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2).
limits: 2023 models; later models may differ. Free-form QA graded by an LLM.
agent_relevance: G5: a critic or judge must not see a proposed answer or a user belief. A challenge prompt alone can flip correct answers.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in CoT
finding: Biasing features in the prompt (for example the answer is always A in few-shot examples) change the answer, and the written reasoning never mentions the bias. Models rationalise the biased wrong answer.
numbers: Accuracy drops by as much as 36% on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks with GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0.
limits: Older models; explanation faithfulness is not the same as answer quality.
agent_relevance: A model-written assumptions list is not a reliable record of what drove the answer. Test assumptions by perturbing inputs in code (G3).

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: A retrieval plus reasoning system forecasts near the human crowd. The best scratchpad prompt tells the model to rephrase the question, list reasons the answer may be no and reasons it may be yes with strength ratings, then aggregate. This is a small form of competing hypotheses.
numbers: Best off-the-shelf model (GPT-4-1106) Brier .208 vs crowd .149 with no retrieval. Full system Brier .179 vs crowd .149 (gap .03); accuracy 71.5% vs crowd 77.0%. Random guess .25. Selective setting beat the crowd.
limits: Binary questions from 5 platforms; test set after model cut-off. I found no clean ablation of the for/against step alone.
agent_relevance: A method from this subfield (argue both sides, rate strengths) already sits inside a forecasting agent loop. Template for a slot-style operator.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: Twelve different LLMs' median forecast matched a human crowd on a 3-month Metaculus tournament. The models showed a yes-leaning (acquiescence) bias and overconfidence.
numbers: Study 1: 31 questions, 1007 forecasts. LLM crowd Brier M=0.20 (SD=0.12) vs human crowd M=0.19 (SD=0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.850, no significant difference.
limits: Small question set (31). Authors report poor calibration of most single models.
agent_relevance: Mixed-model ensembles act like a crowd, but each model leans yes. A devil's-advocate step should target that lean.

source: Anderson, Shah, Kreminski (2024) Homogenization Effects of LLMs on Human Creative Ideation
finding: 36 people brainstormed with ChatGPT or with Oblique Strategies cards. ChatGPT users made more and more detailed ideas, but ideas across users were more alike.
numbers: Group-level similarity: ChatGPT ideas closer to the average embedding (M=.24, SD=.07) vs cards (M=.28, SD=.08), t(32)=2.154, p=.038, d=.47. Categories covered 8.58 vs 6.77, p=.001, d=.54. No difference in unique ideas. Users felt less responsible for ideas.
limits: 36 participants, one task set, 2024 ChatGPT. Individual-level homogenisation not seen.
agent_relevance: Brainstorming with one model widens each person but narrows the group. Several same-model brainstorm runs are not independent.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models
finding: Across 70+ models, open-ended outputs (including brainstorm and ideation queries) repeat inside one model and across different models. Ensembles of models may not give real diversity.
numbers: INFINITY-CHAT: 26K real open-ended queries, 31,250 human annotations. Pairwise similarity between different models 71% to 82% (DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82; vs gpt-4o 0.81). In 79% of cases average within-model similarity exceeds 0.8.
limits: Embedding similarity measure; 25 models detailed in the main paper.
agent_relevance: Hard limit for LLM brainstorming as an SAT. Cuts against the hope in ReConcile and the silicon crowd that model mixing buys independence. Diversity must come from different evidence or code (G4).

source: Perez et al. (2022) Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
finding: A model generates test cases that make another model fail. Zero-shot, few-shot and trained generators found offensive replies at scale, which is machine red teaming.
numbers: 0.5M zero-shot test cases elicited offensive replies 3.7% of the time (18,444 failures). Few-shot and supervised variants raised the rate while keeping some diversity.
limits: Harm-finding task, not analytic judgment. Needs a classifier to say what counts as failure.
agent_relevance: Red team works when a classifier or code decides what a failure is. Fits G2 and G3: the checker, not the model, calls the failure.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Devil's Advocate: Anticipatory Reflection for LLM Agents
finding: Agent loop that, before each action, predicts what could go wrong and prepares a backup, then reviews after the trial. Direct use of devil's advocacy in an agent loop.
numbers: WebArena success rate 23.5% after seven episodes vs LATS 22.7% and Plan+Reflexion 19.8%; abstract: +3.5% over prior zero-shot methods and 45% fewer plan revisions.
limits: WebArena only; gains are a few points. Same model plays the advocate.
agent_relevance: Cheap pre-action 'what could fail' step with a backup plan. Test it against a no-doubt arm (G1).

source: Lee et al. (2025) Amplifying Minority Voices: AI-Mediated Devil's Advocate System for Inclusive Group Decision-Making
finding: A prequel design paper: a 4-agent system (summary, conversation, duplicate checker, paraphrase) lets minority members send private dissent to an LLM that voices it as its own. No results yet.
numbers: No experiment reported; design only. 4 agents.
limits: Position paper with no measured effect. Authors note text-only and fixed-timing limits.
agent_relevance: Shows the human-group form of devil's advocacy turned into an agent role. Nothing measured, so treat as an idea.

source: Chiang et al. (2024) Enhancing AI-Assisted Group Decision Making through LLM-Powered Devil's Advocate (IUI)
finding: Human-AI group decision study where an LLM plays devil's advocate against the AI-assisted group answer. Found by metadata only; the PDF could not be fetched (ACM returned HTML, then 403).
numbers: none read
limits: Not opened. Cannot quote results.
agent_relevance: Candidate to read later: tests an LLM devil's advocate on human groups.

source: RAND (2016) Assessing the Value of Structured Analytic Techniques in the U.S. Intelligence Community
finding: RAND review of SAT evidence in the intelligence community (found in Crossref, not opened). Listed as the human baseline for machine comparisons.
numbers: none read
limits: Not opened here; likely covered in the human-angle files of this folder.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Preprint (2025) The Relationship Between Structured Analytic Techniques and Intelligence Analysis Quality
finding: 2025 preprint on SATs and analysis quality, found in Crossref only. The OSF page would not load.
numbers: none read
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Candidate for the human-evidence angle, not for machines.

source: Search gap note (this run)
finding: I found no study that tests an LLM on Analysis of Competing Hypotheses, a key assumptions check or a premortem as named SATs. WebSearch budget was exhausted, and arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar search endpoints returned 429. Only paper-by-id and Crossref queries worked.
numbers: 0 direct ACH, key-assumptions or premortem LLM studies found.
limits: Absence of evidence in a limited search, not proof none exists.
agent_relevance: Best proxies are the debate, red team, forecasting scratchpad and brainstorming studies above. Testing ACH as an operator would be new work.
